October 13, 2026 <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

MARKETS <\\\/h2>

<\\\/h2>

The cash market is disappearing before our eyes. Some cattle in both Kansas and Texas sold with a negotiated base price of $227 but were not reported in the cash trade. USDA has failed to report any plan to correct non-reporting. The pool of cash continues to dwindle. <\\\/p>

Late trading in the north moved live prices from earlier $218 to $220-$223. Dressed prices were mainly $345 with some up to $350. Some light trade in Texas and Kansas was reported at $226. <\\\/p>

Nebraska is positioned better than Iowa for marketing flexibility. Sustainable Beef in North Platt with newfound profitability is nearing one shift slaughter capacities. Southwestern Kansas beef plants are pulling cattle from the north taking advantage of cheaper prices. Balancing slaughter capacity with fed cattle supplies is always in flux. Supplies of fed cattle are not linear but ebb and flow within a region. Numbers remain tight in the south and prices are likely to continue to hold on to premiums. <\\\/p>

The year on year advances in carcass weights are due to end this year. The large spreads between this year and prior year will cease acheiving premiums to last year. There remains a target out weight that will max out the conversion of feed into muscle. Genetics continues to be important but high YG 4&5s are troubling processors to deliver efficient cuts to the retailer as well as presenting marketing problems with the large cuts. In 2027 it will be likely we will see an end to carcass weight gains over the current level. <\\\/p>

This week slaughter volumes was 535,000 head - 13,000 under the previous week and in line with current retail demand for beef. It fell 17,000 under last year. Plant attendance is normal and changes in weekly slaughter will be driven by supply and demand. Processors have maintained profitability since July - the longest period during the past few years. The status for fed supplies will remain tight through year end especially in the south. <\\\/p>

Benchmarking <\\\/a> . On Tuesday of each week, USDA releases a weighted average price report for all cattle sold the previous week. The report summarizes the distributed price levels for each category of sale such as Negotiated\\\/Formula\\\/Forward Contracts. Beef producers are able to measure the marketing price for their cattle compared to the national averages. <\\\/p>

The Comprehensive Fed Cattle Weekly Report <\\\/a> offers the most current information on the current status of fed cattle being harvested. The report is published each Tuesday and includes the previous weeks change in carcass weights and quality grading. The latest report shows carcass weights at 952#, flat with the prior week, and 16# heavier than last year. The combined steer and heifer weights can easily be influenced when the proportion of steers to heifers in the weekly slaughter changes. Quality grade was down .1% from the previous week at 87.2. The quality grade remains near historic highs as cattle are fed to heavier weights. <\\\/p>

The Weekly Steer and Heifer Grading Report <\\\/a> <\\\/a> reflects regional supplies of choice and prime cattle and often is determinative of regional differences in live prices. The report also indicates the current status of fed cattle offerings in each area. <\\\/p>

Forward Cattle Contracts <\\\/a> : Forward contracts are always a portion of the inventories the processors maintain for slaughter. Offered basis levels will move up and down as processors want to add to forward contracts or not. The driver in forward purchases of cattle will always be forward sales of beef. Packers will always be willing to take a price risk off the producers plate in return for an extra margin. The movement of futures prices, either up or down, will relate to the number of forward contracts. <\\\/p>

Formula and Negotiated Grids. The Price and Distribution Report <\\\/a> delineates the various selling methods and net results. <\\\/p>

The Cattle Contracts Report <\\\/a> details the percent of contracts by volume of cattle and by number of contracts for selling cattle. Formula selling that was once the largest marketing method and still is, but is losing ground to negotiated grids where the premiums and discounts are set but the base price is negotiated. <\\\/p>

Spreads between choice offerings and prime cuts historically have been wide and with more product and difficulty moving expensive cuts, many Prime cuts now sell at smaller incremental price spreads to choice causing many consumers to upgrade their purchases. Casualities in this change have been branded or all natural products that are commonly passed over by consumers. <\\\/p>

The Cutout <\\\/a> . Box prices firmed in early week trading. The lean beef prices have struggled to hold ground under pressure from the imported beef. This past weeks slaughter volume jumped from the previous weeks small number to the largest volume since January. Slaughter volumes will continue to be dictated by processing margins and government intervention. <\\\/p>

It is important to remember that spot box prices are much like spot cash prices for live cattle. Most boxes are sold under formulas and do not always have the same fluctuations as the spot market. <\\\/p>

Replacement markets <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

October and November are the largest marketing periods of the year for replacement cattle. Demand for replacements is high and recent rains provided broad coverage of the nation leading to new grazing opportunities for cattle for growing and breeding. Those buyers closely examining the future outcome of todays purchases, based on deferred cattle futures, will not find financial rewards at the end of the line. <\\\/p>

Weather will always influence the market for replacement cattle. The main grain belt in the southern plains, where many cattle are grazed on winter wheat, has enjoyed generous rains. Most fields have been planted and some have an emerged crop. Warm weather will now be important to plant growth and grazing opportunities. The wildcard for a year that could provide the largest winter grazing in decades is availability of cattle. There simply may not be enough cattle to stock winter grazing sites. Recent rains in the desert southwest has activated hopes for desert grazing and the opening of the border will provide some limited supply of cattle. <\\\/p>

Movement from Mexico has featured groups of heavy cattle nearing finish in Mexican feedlots. These cattle will move to U.S. feedyards for a short finishing period before being sold to processors. Very few light Mexican cattle are being offered because of generous rains across Chihuahua and Sonora. <\\\/p>

Seasonally health problems, that can occur anytime with the stress of weaning, worsen for unweaned calves during the fall. Many operators have suffered the penalty paid when they buy fresh weaned calves and experience usually large death loss. Not only can death loss percentages jump, but also sick calves present a constant labor requirement and long term performance impairment. A $50 cwt. spread between weaned and unweaned calves is large, but sometimes justified. The spreads between weaned and unweaned calves is widening. Knowing more about the background of new purchases can be helpful including full health records. <\\\/p>

The Drought Monitor <\\\/a> is a map showing regions of the country under stress for lack of normal rainfall. The map is compiled over a week and updated every Thursday with data collected through Tuesday of that week. <\\\/p>

October 15, 2026 <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

MARKETS <\\\/h2>

<\\\/h2>

Texas sold a pen of cattle online yesterday for $226 - steady with last week. Packers stand ready to extend inventories at steady prices but are hesitant to raise prices unless forced - hoping to hold on to margins that have left them profitable for the past two months. Packer inventories are short making it likely they will purchase some cattle today. <\\\/p>

The cash market is disappearing before our eyes. Show lists were larger in Texas and Kansas but smaller in Nebraska. Ideas are developing that northern feedlots are more current than the past few weeks. Some cattle in both Kansas and Texas sold with a negotiated base price of $227 last week but were not reported in the cash trade. USDA has failed to release any plan to correct non-reporting. The pool of cash transactions continues to dwindle. <\\\/p>

One unique feature of beef demand has been resilience. High prices normally with most products cause buyers to switch to other alternatives, buy cheaper versions of the same product, eat less of the product or stop eating it. Beef demand in large part has survived the price increases of the last two years. That doesnt mean demand cant be damaged in the future by price, but it is a reflection of the importance most consumers place on the desirability of the product. Economists would call the demand curve for beef largely inelastic. <\\\/p>

Inflation risks will remain in the news causing additional increases in interest rates. The most recent 3.7% increase in the CPI will assure additional interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve bank - probably this year. <\\\/p>

<\\\/p>

This week slaughter volumes was 535,000 head - 13,000 under the previous week and in line with current retail demand for beef. It fell 17,000 under last year. Plant attendance is normal and changes in weekly slaughter will be driven by supply and demand. Processors have maintained profitability since July - the longest period during the past few years. The status for fed supplies will remain tight through year end especially in the south. <\\\/p>

More details will be available this weekend in this weeks editorial. <\\\/p>

Replacement markets <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

October and November are the largest marketing periods of the year for replacement cattle. Much of the nations farm tracts will be left empty of cattle reserving the crop to be harvested for grain. <\\\/p>
